title: Arts & Music
summary: Music and the arts: how music works, and how to play it.

children.title: Music Theory
children.summary: Music theory explains why music sounds the way it does: how pitches relate, how rhythm is organised, how chords move and how whole pieces are built.

children.title: Sound and Pitch
children.summary: Music is organised sound.

children.title: The Harmonic Series
children.summary: A plucked string or a blown pipe vibrates at its fundamental frequency and at every whole-number multiple of it at once.

children.title: Notation
children.summary: Western music is written on a five-line staff: vertical position shows pitch and the shape of each note shows its length.

children.title: Rhythm and Meter
children.summary: Rhythm is how sounds are placed in time.

children.title: Meter and Time Signatures
children.summary: Meter is the regular grouping of beats into bars (measures), with the first beat of each bar the strongest.

children.title: Syncopation, Tuplets and Polyrhythm
children.summary: Rhythm becomes interesting when it pulls against the meter.

children.title: Intervals
children.summary: An interval is the distance between two pitches.

children.title: Consonance and Dissonance
children.summary: Some intervals sound stable and smooth (consonant), others tense or rough (dissonant).

children.title: Scales and Keys
children.summary: A scale is a set of pitches arranged in order within an octave.

children.title: Minor Scales
children.summary: The minor mode lowers the third scale degree, and usually the sixth and seventh too.

children.title: Key Signatures and the Circle of Fifths
children.summary: Each step up a perfect fifth adds one sharp to the key signature; each step down a fifth adds one flat.

children.title: The Modes
children.summary: Start the major scale's pattern of steps from a different note and you get a mode.

children.title: Other Scales
children.summary: Beyond major, minor and the modes, a handful of other scales turn up again and again: the pentatonic scales of folk and rock, the blues scale, and the symmetric scales of Debussy, Messiaen and jazz.

children.title: Chords
children.summary: A chord is three or more notes sounded together.

children.title: Inversions and Figured Bass
children.summary: A chord keeps its name whichever note is lowest, but the bass note changes how it sounds and how it can be used.

children.title: Extended and Altered Chords
children.summary: Keep stacking thirds above a seventh chord and you reach ninths, elevenths and thirteenths.

children.title: Harmony
children.summary: Harmony is how chords follow one another.

children.title: Cadences
children.summary: A cadence is the harmonic punctuation at the end of a phrase.

children.title: Voice Leading
children.summary: Voice leading is the art of moving each note of one chord to a note of the next so that every part makes a good melody of its own and the parts stay independent.

children.title: Non-Chord Tones
children.summary: Melodies are not made only of chord notes.

children.title: Secondary Dominants and Tonicization
children.summary: Any major or minor chord in a key can be made to sound briefly like a tonic by putting its own dominant before it.

children.title: Modulation
children.summary: A modulation moves the tonal centre to a new key, confirmed by a cadence there.

children.title: Chromatic Harmony
children.summary: Beyond secondary dominants, tonal music borrows chords from the parallel minor, colours the predominant with the Neapolitan sixth and the augmented sixth chords, and decorates with common-tone diminished sevenths.

children.title: Counterpoint
children.summary: Counterpoint is the craft of combining melodies that are independent yet sound good together.

children.title: Imitation, Canon and Fugue
children.summary: When one voice repeats a melody that another has just played, the music is imitative.

children.title: Form
children.summary: Form is how a piece is put together over time: small ideas grouped into phrases, phrases into sections, sections into a whole.

children.title: Classical Forms
children.summary: Most instrumental music from about 1700 to 1900 follows a handful of forms.

children.title: Popular Forms
children.summary: Blues, jazz standards and pop songs have their own forms: the 12-bar blues, the 32-bar AABA song and the verse–chorus song.

children.title: Jazz Harmony
children.summary: Jazz harmony takes the chords of tonal music, adds sevenths, ninths and beyond as normal colour, and organises improvisation around chord symbols and the scales that fit them.

children.title: Reharmonization
children.summary: Jazz players rarely play a tune's chords as written.

children.title: Tuning and Temperament
children.summary: How exactly should the notes of a scale be tuned?

children.title: Temperaments
children.summary: A temperament adjusts ('tempers') some pure intervals so the rest fit.

children.title: Post-Tonal Theory
children.summary: Much twentieth-century music abandons the tonal centre.

children.title: Twelve-Tone Technique
children.summary: Schoenberg's twelve-tone method orders all twelve pitch classes into a row and builds a piece from that row and its transformations, so that no pitch class is emphasised as a tonic.

children.title: Guitar
children.summary: The guitar is a fretted string instrument: six strings over a neck divided by metal frets into semitones.

children.title: Tuning, Tab and Chord Diagrams
children.summary: Standard tuning sets the six strings to E A D G B E, from low to high.

children.title: Basic Technique
children.summary: Playing the guitar is two jobs: the fretting hand chooses the pitch, the picking hand starts the sound and shapes its rhythm.

children.title: Guitar Theory
children.summary: Guitar theory is ordinary music theory, the same intervals, scales and chords as on the piano, seen through the fretboard.

children.title: The Fretboard
children.summary: Every fret is a semitone and every string is a fourth (or, G to B, a major third) above the one below.

children.title: Intervals as Shapes
children.summary: On the guitar every interval is a fixed fingering that works anywhere on the neck, apart from one shift at the B string.

children.title: Scales on the Guitar
children.summary: A scale on the guitar is a pattern of frets in one hand position, repeated across the strings.

children.title: The CAGED System
children.summary: The five open major chords C, A, G, E and D are also five movable shapes.

children.title: Chord Voicings
children.summary: A voicing is a particular arrangement of a chord's notes.

children.title: Harmony and Progressions
children.summary: Harmony on the guitar is the same Roman-numeral harmony as on the piano (see Harmony (#/arts/music-theory/harmony)), but guitarists think of it through movable shapes, the capo and the Nashville number system.

children.title: Soloing over Chords
children.summary: Improvising on the guitar is choosing notes that fit the chord of the moment.
